evidence.note: The answer proposes preservation and links each ship to its building location.

segments.summary: A modern return would likely preserve both Nelson-class battleships near the communities that built them.
segments.question: What would happen if HMS Rodney and HMS Nelson were teleported to the present day?
segments.answerShort: Both would probably become museum ships, ideally near their original Tyneside and Birkenhead builders.

segments.title: The 16-inch shells adapted into Pearl Harbor bombs
segments.body: The panel identifies the heavy armor-piercing bombs used at Pearl Harbor as conversions from 16-inch shells. Japan had 14- and 16-inch battleship weapons rather than a 15-inch service caliber, so a 15-inch origin does not fit the fleet's ammunition. The exchange then tests what 15-inch guns on the Kongo class would imply for the earlier naval balance. British planners would be far less willing to abandon the G3 battlecruisers before negotiating a treaty if Japanese fast capital ships already carried weapons of that size. The short correction therefore connects ordnance identification with the competitive logic behind interwar capital-ship programs.

evidence.note: The panel corrects the shell caliber and links a hypothetical 15-inch Kongo class to completion of the British G3s.

segments.summary: Japan converted 16-inch naval shells rather than nonexistent 15-inch ammunition, prompting a related counterfactual about British G3 construction.
segments.question: Were the Japanese battleship shells converted into Pearl Harbor bombs 15-inch or 16-inch weapons?
segments.answerShort: They were 16-inch shells; Japan did not field a 15-inch battleship gun from which to take them.

segments.title: Why the slowest wartime warship has no simple answer
segments.body: The panel cannot name one slowest warship without first defining the category. Sailing commerce raiders could make only single-digit speeds, while some monitors and armed trawlers were also exceptionally slow under their own power. Towed flak barges complicate the question further because they carried weapons but did not necessarily operate as independent ships. Even for powered vessels, an official top speed may differ from what the hull actually achieved in service. The useful result is therefore a classification warning rather than a false precision: ship type, propulsion, and the chosen measure of speed must be fixed before candidates can be compared.

evidence.note: The panel considers sailing raiders, monitors, barges, trawlers, and the difference between official and actual speed.

segments.summary: The answer changes with the boundary between ships and boats, powered and sailing craft, and official versus achieved speed.
segments.question: What was the warship with the lowest top speed in the First or Second World War?
segments.answerShort: There is no single answer until warship, independent propulsion, and official versus actual top speed are defined.

segments.title: Why Royal Navy air-defense ships become destroyers
segments.body: The Royal Navy wanted a larger hull with taller masts, longer radar horizon, and more missiles than a conventional frigate could provide. In the Horizon program, Britain effectively wanted a destroyer called a frigate, while France and Italy wanted a genuine frigate. Those different operational aims produced requirements that were technically negotiable but institutionally difficult to reconcile.

evidence.note: Comparison of British Type 45 requirements with French and Italian Horizon aims.

segments.summary: Radar height, missile capacity, and divergent missions pushed Britain's air-defense requirement beyond a true frigate.
segments.question: Why did the anti-aircraft frigate idea not work out for the Royal Navy?
segments.answerShort: Britain's radar and missile requirements demanded a destroyer-sized ship, unlike the smaller frigate sought by its Horizon partners.

segments.title: Can a sleeping watch ground a warship?
segments.body: The panel confirms that sleeping on watch has caused groundings or related accidents in the past. It characterizes the event as unusual because more than one person is normally assigned to monitor the ship and keep the team alert. The brief answer shows why watchkeeping is organized around overlapping human checks rather than a single individual's endurance.

evidence.note: The answer confirms past cases and points to multiple watchstanders as the normal safeguard.

segments.summary: It has happened, but multiple watchstanders normally provide the human redundancy that makes such failures uncommon.
segments.question: Have naval watches fallen asleep and caused a grounding or another serious incident?
segments.answerShort: Yes, but it is rare because several people are normally on watch and able to keep one another alert.

segments.title: Why naval historians still need archive research trips
segments.body: Many primary sources have never been digitized, and digitized collections may reproduce only part of a file. Scanning decisions can crop annotations, reverse sides, enclosures, or adjacent documents that explain why the main item was created. A researcher working only from an online image may therefore miss context that becomes obvious when handling the complete archival folder. The answer makes travel part of evidence control rather than academic ritual: visiting the archive allows the historian to check completeness and follow connections that a catalog or selected scan cannot expose.

evidence.note: The panel explains incomplete digitization and the loss of relevant material when documents are selectively scanned.

segments.summary: Digitization remains incomplete and often omits marginal material needed to understand a document in context.
segments.question: Why are research trips still necessary when many archival sources are online?
segments.answerShort: Because much remains undigitized and even available scans can omit the surrounding material needed to interpret a source correctly.

segments.title: Why treaty battleships studied 16-inch twin turrets
segments.body: At very large calibers, three triple turrets generally save weight and provide nine guns compared with the barbettes and machinery required for four twin turrets carrying eight. Treaty studies nevertheless used twins when designers needed a narrower beam and could exploit extra hull length. Without the 35,000-ton constraint, the broader and more efficient triple arrangement became easier to justify, as in later Lion-class thinking.

evidence.note: The panel compares beam, length, barbette weight, and gun count for twin and triple layouts.

segments.summary: Twin turrets could preserve a narrow beam under treaty limits even when triples were more weight-efficient overall.
segments.question: Why did the Royal Navy study 16-inch twin turrets in the 1920s if triples were more efficient?
segments.answerShort: Twins allowed a slimmer beam under treaty limits, trading extra length and machinery for a hull shape that could meet the displacement constraint.

segments.title: The tradeoff between shared and independent gun cradles
segments.body: Mounting several guns on one cradle simplifies elevation machinery, lets the barrels sit closer together, and reduces turret size and weight. The cost is that one failure can disable the complete group and the closely spaced guns can interact unfavorably in flight. Independent cradles add machinery and space but provide better durability because a hit or malfunction may remove only one weapon. Armored partitions in ships such as the Iowa class reinforce that damage isolation. The panel also distinguishes catastrophic penetration from ordinary battle friction: shock, recoil, and small mechanical faults can stop equipment even when armor remains intact. Modern preference for single mounts reflects improved reliability and limited-war priorities, while older designs often accepted some accuracy loss to gain volume of fire.

evidence.note: Comparison of weight, space, reliability, damage isolation, recoil, accuracy, and changing modern design priorities.

segments.summary: Shared cradles save weight and space, while independent mountings preserve guns after damage or mechanical failure.
segments.question: Why mount naval guns on a shared cradle instead of giving each barrel independent elevation?
segments.answerShort: A shared cradle is smaller, lighter, and simpler, but independent mountings are more resistant to damage and mechanical failure.

segments.title: Why a triple five-inch gun does not fit existing Arleigh Burkes
segments.body: A hypothetical future Arleigh Burke flight could be designed from the outset for a triple five-inch mount. Retrofitting existing Flight II or Flight III ships is a different problem because the added weapon and supporting structure impose major weight and space demands. The panel expects the conversion to require removing or sharply reducing vertical-launch cells. That trade would undermine the missile capacity central to the destroyer's role, making the upgrade self-defeating. The answer illustrates why a weapon that fits on paper can still be incompatible with a completed ship's weight and mission balance.

evidence.note: The answer allows a purpose-designed future flight but rejects retrofits that would delete or severely reduce VLS cells.

segments.summary: The mount's weight and internal demand would consume too much missile capacity unless a future flight were designed around it.
segments.question: Could Flight II or Flight III Arleigh Burke destroyers be upgraded with a triple five-inch mount?
segments.answerShort: No practical retrofit is likely; it would cost too much VLS capacity, although a future flight could be designed around the mount.

segments.title: Why equal post-Jutland fleets would fail at Washington
segments.body: A five-five-five settlement could be militarily cleaner, but American negotiators would not accept Japan receiving the same capital-ship strength as Britain and the United States. A more plausible five-five-three formula would allow Britain several Nelson- or F3-type ships, the United States to finish part of the Colorado program, and Japan a smaller modern force. Even then, delegates would dispute what counted as a post-Jutland design.

evidence.note: The answer compares five-five-five with five-five-three and discusses likely ship programs.

segments.summary: Equal five-ship allowances might simplify fleets but were politically impossible because the United States would reject Japanese parity.
segments.question: Would giving Britain, the United States, and Japan five post-Jutland capital ships each have been better than the historical treaty?
segments.answerShort: It might produce cleaner fleets, but Japanese parity was politically unacceptable; a five-five-three compromise was the realistic ceiling.

segments.title: Who takes Arizona's place in Battleship Row?
segments.body: Removing Arizona for a Bremerton refit changes the geometry of Battleship Row rather than removing the Japanese attack plan. Nevada could shift into Arizona's berth, making her the most direct candidate to receive the heavy armor-piercing bombs aimed there. A different mooring arrangement might instead move Oklahoma or West Virginia from a double berth into the exposed position. Some bombs would also be redistributed once the attacking aircraft encountered a different target pattern. The answer emphasizes that Pearl Harbor damage depended on where individual ships were moored as well as on their intrinsic protection.

evidence.note: The panel reconstructs Battleship Row and considers Nevada, Oklahoma, or West Virginia in Arizona's place.

segments.summary: Nevada is the likeliest ship to occupy the empty berth, although changing the double-berthing pattern could expose Oklahoma or West Virginia instead.
segments.question: If USS Arizona were being refitted at Bremerton on 7 December 1941, which ship would take her place under the Japanese bombers?
segments.answerShort: Probably Nevada, although Oklahoma or West Virginia could occupy the exposed berth if the battleship moorings were rearranged.

segments.title: When older warships fight in roles they were not built to survive
segments.body: The Invincible-class battlecruisers were poorly suited to the punishment they faced at Jutland, yet they were committed because commanders needed available numbers. The same general problem recurs when navies fight with the fleet on hand rather than the one they would prefer. In the Falklands, Britain would have wanted more Sea Wolf-equipped frigates but instead deployed several ships whose Sea Slug or Sea Cat systems reflected an earlier technological generation.

evidence.note: The closing exchange cites the Invincible class and Falklands-era frigate defenses.

segments.summary: The closing answer compares the Invincible-class at Jutland with older air-defense frigates sent to the Falklands.
segments.question: What are examples of technologically weaker ships being used where they should not have been?
segments.answerShort: The Invincible class at Jutland and older British air-defense ships in the Falklands show how operational necessity forces outdated vessels into high-threat roles.
